title: Wonder Leads to Wisdom
author: Christopher Perrin
summary: Christopher Perrin, founder of Classical Academic Press, takes up what Mortimer Adler ranked among the 102 Great Ideas, how does a person become wise, and argues classical education has always answered it the same way: not through age alone, since Aristotle held practical wisdom impossible for the young, but through study of what is old, guided by teachers who model wisdom as noble friends rather than pursue novelty for its own sake. Drawing on Anthony Kronman's critique of the modern research university in Education's End, Perrin contrasts old professors who "died a happy death" knowing they had transmitted a treasured inheritance with modern academics chasing a novel contribution that "at least 99 of 100" fail to make, arguing the classical model of teacher as wisdom-transmitter has been displaced by one that mostly produces unread journal articles. He builds his central image from a medieval mosaic floor in Siena's cathedral depicting the mountain of wisdom, where Lady Wisdom hands a palm branch to Socrates, using it to explain why Classical Academic Press changed its company motto to "Wonder to Wisdom": citing Aristotle's Metaphysics on wonder as philosophy's origin and Sertillanges's account of academic work beginning in a moment of ecstatic self-forgetting, Perrin frames wonder and wisdom as the two poles of a genuinely good education, illustrated finally by Raphael's painting of Prudence, a young woman with a second face looking backward, gaining wisdom precisely by examining the accumulated experience of the past.
points: Perrin's central critique of the modern research university, drawn from Kronman's Education's End, is precise and damning: professors who chase 'a novel contribution to their discipline' mostly fail ('at least 99 of 100'), unlike old professors who transmitted 'a great, treasured inheritance' and 'died a happy death' knowing they had blessed their students.

The Siena cathedral mosaic (Lady Wisdom handing a palm branch to Socrates, a Latin inscription urging pilgrims to 'climb the rough mountain') is used as a physical, walkable metaphor for education itself, letting Perrin argue that Christian and classical-pagan wisdom traditions were understood by medieval builders as complementary stages of one ascent, not rivals.

The reframe of wonder via Aristotle's Metaphysics (philosophy begins in wondering 'at the obvious difficulties') and Sertillanges's account of academic ecstasy as 'a forgetting to live our own poor life' gives Classical Academic Press's rebranded motto, 'Wonder to Wisdom,' a specific philosophical genealogy rather than treating it as a marketing slogan.

The closing image of Raphael's Prudence, personified with two faces, one looking in a mirror and one looking backward at an old man, literalizes the essay's thesis: a person becomes wise not chiefly through self-examination in isolation, but by looking backward at 'the accumulated experience of the ages' and knowing oneself through that inheritance.
quotes: Modern professors, charmed by ideals of making a novel contribution to their discipline and advancing the march of knowledge, don't die a happy death, for they have tried to contribute something truly novel to our accumulated store of knowledge and failed. At least 99 of 100 fail. Who reads their journal articles?
For this they need models to imitate, and this is precisely Kronman's point about what the old professors sought to be: mature students calling younger students to seek and find wisdom.

For it is owing to their wonder that men both now begin and at first began to philosophize; they wondered originally at the obvious difficulties, then advanced little by little and stated difficulties about the greater matters.
Every academic work begins by a moment of ecstasy; only in the second place does the talent of arrangement, the technique of transitions, connection of ideas, construction, come into play.
It turns out she has two faces and one is the face of an old man looking backwards. She is wise because she has looked backwards at what is old, history.

In the classical tradition, wonder leads to wisdom. Yes, there is an entire life between the two, but these are the two classic poles, the beginning and the end. It should describe a full life; it describes a good education.
